name: Color analysis

angle.text: Users have their skin tone, hair and eyes assigned to a season, then wear clothing and makeup in that palette so colors near the face flatter them. The visible effect of a color is immediate; little rigorous research backs the specific four-season categories.

summary: Seasonal colour analysis: matching clothing and makeup palettes to skin undertone, hair and eyes; popular and low-risk, but little rigorous research backs its specific categories.
note: Different analysts and apps can assign the same person to different seasons; published validation is sparse.
currentQuick:
Color analysis sorts people into palettes, traditionally the four seasons of spring, summer, autumn and winter, based on skin undertone, hair and eye colour. Followers wear the colours assigned to their season in the belief that these make skin look clearer and the face more harmonious.
The method was popularised in the early 1980s and went viral again on TikTok in the early 2020s. Its categories are widely used but have little peer-reviewed validation.
How it works: Practitioners hold coloured fabric near the face, usually in daylight, and judge how it affects skin, eyes and overall contrast. Variants add dimensions such as undertone, lightness and chroma, expanding the four seasons to twelve or more sub-seasons.
Risks and caveats: There is no physical risk. Critics cited in encyclopedia coverage point to subjectivity, oversimplified categories, paid consultations and the encouragement of buying new clothes. Early systems were criticised for centring white clients.
deepLead:
Color analysis, usually called seasonal color analysis, is a system that advises people which colours to wear based on features such as skin tone, hair and eye colour. People are typically assigned to one of four seasons, winter, summer, spring or autumn, with winters and summers described as having blue undertones and springs and autumns yellow ones .
The modern system was standardised by consultant Carole Jackson, whose 1980 book Color Me Beautiful was a bestseller, building on earlier work by figures including Johannes Itten . It resurfaced in the early 2020s as a viral trend on TikTok . In looksmaxxing and style communities it is treated as a low-cost way to improve appearance through clothing and makeup choices.
Published scientific support for the specific season categories is limited. Encyclopedia summaries note some research that people prefer clothing hues harmonising with their skin tone and that colours influence mood, while describing the practice as having few rigorous peer-reviewed studies behind its core claims .

name: Voice maxxing

angle.text: Users practise pitch, resonance and delivery techniques, borrowed from speech therapy, to sound deeper or more masculine and come across as more attractive. Speech-therapy methods exist for voice change; no trials test them for attractiveness.

summary: Working on pitch, resonance and delivery to sound more attractive or masculine; speech-therapy techniques exist, but no trials test it for attractiveness.
note: Voice therapy is established for medical use; its use for attractiveness has not been studied in trials.
currentQuick:
Voice-maxxing is the looksmaxxing practice of changing how one sounds, most often aiming for a deeper, more resonant voice. Looksmax.org has long-running threads on whether a deep voice raises attractiveness and how to acquire one.
Speech-language pathologists use voice therapy to alter pitch, resonance and voice quality for medical and gender-voice purposes, but no published trial has tested it as an attractiveness intervention.
How it works: Voice pitch is set largely by vocal fold length and tension, with typical adult male speech around 90 to 155 Hz and female around 165 to 255 Hz. Therapy approaches work on breathing, resonance and pitch habits rather than the anatomy itself.
Risks and caveats: Training itself is low risk when taught by a clinician; forceful pitch-lowering can strain the voice, and therapy sources emphasise vocal hygiene. Surgical or hormonal changes to the voice are separate medical topics.
deepLead:
Voice-maxxing refers to deliberate changes to pitch, resonance, and speaking style, usually to sound deeper or more masculine, in order to be perceived as more attractive or authoritative. It is a common subtopic on looksmax.org, where threads ask whether a deep voice increases attractiveness and how much .
Typical adult male speech has a fundamental frequency of about 90 to 155 Hz and typical adult female speech about 165 to 255 Hz . Voice therapy, delivered by speech-language pathologists, uses techniques such as resonant voice therapy to change vocal quality, and is used in transgender voice care, voice disorders and vocal hygiene .

name: Dripmaxxing / fashion

angle.text: Users improve clothing, fit, accessories and styling to look better without changing the face or body, and the difference shows as soon as they are dressed. It is a low-cost approach discussed in forums, with no clinical research behind it.

summary: Dressing and styling to look better; a low-cost softmax with no clinical research behind it.
note: Evidence on clothing and perceived attractiveness is indirect; spending on hype brands is optional.
currentQuick:
Dripmaxxing means improving how you look through clothes, fit and accessories instead of surgery or products. The word "drip" is hip-hop slang for stylish dress.
It is discussed in looksmaxxing communities as one of the easiest, reversible changes. No clinical trials exist on it.
How it works: Proponents say clothing shapes first impressions and can flatter body proportions. Psychology research on how clothing affects the wearer (enclothed cognition) has had mixed replication results.
Risks and caveats: No medical risks. The main caveat is cost, particularly where hype brands and resale markets are involved.
deepLead:
Dripmaxxing is the looksmaxxing-community term for improving one's appearance through clothing, accessories and styling rather than through changes to the face or body. "Drip" is internet and hip-hop slang for stylish dress, and the "-maxxing" suffix marks a deliberate effort to optimise it. Forum discussions typically cover outfit choice, fit, brands and the idea that dressing well can raise how attractive a person is perceived to be.
The wiki's source base for the term itself is thin: the main community threads that use the word contain slurs or explicit content and are not cited here. Most of what can be documented comes from background research on streetwear culture and on the psychology of clothing .
Published research on clothing and appearance is mixed. The most-cited experiment on how clothing affects the wearer, the 2012 "enclothed cognition" study, has had replication difficulties . No clinical studies exist on dripmaxxing as such.

name: Beard maxxing

angle.text: Users grow and shape a beard to frame the jaw, disguise a recessed chin or add masculinity, and the change is visible as the beard fills in. Minoxidil or transplants are sometimes discussed for patchy growth. Research on beards and attractiveness is mixed.

summary: Growing and shaping facial hair to frame the jaw; cheap and reversible, with mixed research on attractiveness.
note: Shaving can cause pseudofolliculitis barbae; transplants are surgical.
currentQuick:
Beard maxxing means growing, trimming or enhancing facial hair to change how the lower face looks. Forum users call it one of the cheapest looksmaxes and discuss styles for different jaw shapes.
Research cited by Wikipedia suggests bearded faces are rated as more dominant, but how beards affect attractiveness is not settled.
How it works: Beard growth is driven by androgens such as DHT and genetics. A beard adds a hair outline to the jaw and chin, which proponents say changes how the lower face reads. Medical options for sparse growth include minoxidil (studied in one placebo-controlled trial) and beard hair transplants.
Risks and caveats: Beard grooming carries minor risks such as ingrown hairs; pseudofolliculitis barbae is a documented shaving-related condition. Transplants are surgery with the usual procedural risks.
deepLead:
Beard maxxing is the looksmaxxing practice of growing, shaping or enhancing facial hair to change how the lower face and jawline appear. Community members describe a beard as one of the cheapest and most visible changes a man can make, and discuss styles aimed at framing the jaw, disguising a weak chin or short ramus, or adding perceived masculinity .
Beard growth is driven by androgens, mainly dihydrotestosterone, and is partly genetic . Methods discussed in the community range from grooming and styling to topical minoxidil and, in medical practice, beard hair transplantation . Evidence on how beards affect attractiveness is mixed and the wiki records both what proponents and what researchers report.

name: Squintmaxxing

angle.text: Proponents narrow the eyelids slightly, in photos and in daily habit, to get the intense look called hunter eyes. It is a free, instant adjustment, though its effect on ratings and attractiveness is untested and based on anecdote.

summary: Habitually narrowing the eyes for a "hunter" look; free, reversible and untested.
note: No studies on appearance effects; community claims about hair loss are unsupported by research.
currentQuick:
Squintmaxxing means slightly narrowing the eyelids, often, to get a more intense "hunter eyes" look. It costs nothing and can be stopped at any time.
It is promoted on looksmax.org, but no research has tested whether it changes perceived attractiveness.
How it works: Narrowing the lids lowers the visible upper eyelid line and reduces the amount of eye shown. Proponents say this changes the impression of the eye area.
Risks and caveats: Squinting is generally regarded as harmless, with temporary headache from muscle tension the harm cited by an ophthalmologist. Forum claims about wrinkles or temple balding have no published support.
deepLead:
Squintmaxxing is a looksmaxxing practice in which a person habitually narrows the eyelids slightly, aiming for the look community members call "hunter eyes": a lower upper eyelid line and a more intense, less wide-open gaze. Proponents describe it as a free, instant adjustment that can make the eye area look more attractive .
Squinting itself is a documented behaviour. Wikipedia notes it can briefly sharpen vision in people with uncorrected refractive error, and an ophthalmologist quoted there says the belief that squinting damages eyesight is an old wives' tale, with temporary headache from muscle tension the only harm cited . No studies have tested whether deliberate squinting changes perceived attractiveness.

name: Dental work / teeth maxxing

angle.text: Users whiten teeth with strips, pastes and dentist treatments, often alongside orthodontics, for a brighter and neater smile. Peroxide whitening products have clinical trial support, and the shade change is visible after use.

summary: Whitening and tidying teeth; peroxide products have trial support, with sensitivity as the usual trade-off.
note: Sensitivity and gum irritation are common; regulators cap peroxide strength in retail products.
currentQuick:
Teeth maxxing means improving how teeth look, mostly by whitening them with strips, pastes, trays or dentist treatments. It is among the more evidence-backed softmaxes.
Randomized trials and reviews show peroxide whitening changes tooth colour. Forum users also discuss DIY methods that have not been studied.
How it works: Hydrogen peroxide or carbamide peroxide breaks down pigment molecules in the tooth. Whitening toothpastes mainly remove surface stains with abrasives.
Risks and caveats: Tooth sensitivity is frequently reported, and strong peroxide can irritate or burn gums. Regulators limit peroxide strength in retail products; over-abrasive products can damage tooth tissue.
deepLead:
Teeth maxxing is the looksmaxxing practice of improving the colour and look of the teeth, most often through whitening. Community discussion centres on whitening strips, toothpastes, dentist treatments and do-it-yourself methods, often alongside orthodontics and other dental work .
Tooth whitening typically uses hydrogen peroxide or carbamide peroxide, which break down pigment molecules . Reviews and trials describe clear colour changes, with tooth sensitivity and gum irritation as the most commonly reported side effects, and regulators limit peroxide concentrations in retail products .

name: Hair dye / bleaching hair

angle.text: Users dye or bleach scalp hair, eyebrows, lashes or facial hair to change contrast, cover grey, or make sparse brows and beards look darker and fuller. The colour change is visible straight after application and is a common cosmetic practice.

summary: Dyeing or bleaching hair for colour and contrast; common cosmetic practice with documented allergy risk.
note: PPD allergy can be severe; bleaching peroxide can damage hair and skin.
currentQuick:
Hair dyeing and bleaching change hair colour using chemical colourants or lighteners. Looksmaxxers use them for hair, brows and facial hair.
The chemistry is well documented. Research on harms centres on allergy, with mixed evidence on cancer.
How it works: Permanent dyes use ammonia and peroxide to open the cuticle and form colour in the hair; bleach oxidises melanin. Semi-permanent and temporary dyes coat or sit under the cuticle and wash out.
Risks and caveats: PPD allergy can cause itching, burning and sores, sometimes delayed. IARC lists some ingredients as mutagenic or carcinogenic, though overall evidence linking dye use to cancer is described as limited and inconsistent. The EU restricts many dye chemicals.
deepLead:
Hair dyeing and bleaching change the colour of scalp hair, eyebrows, lashes or facial hair with chemical colourants or lighteners. In looksmaxxing communities they are discussed as ways to adjust contrast, cover grey, darken sparse eyebrows or beard, or change overall look .
Dyes are classed by permanence: permanent dyes use ammonia and a peroxide developer and can lighten, while semi-permanent and temporary dyes deposit colour without lightening . The main documented harm is allergic contact dermatitis, especially to para-phenylenediamine (PPD), and cancer associations remain debated .

name: Carrot maxxing

chain: Carotenoids build up in outer skin
angle.text: Users eat large amounts of carrots and other carotenoid-rich foods to give the skin a golden glow without sun exposure. Carotenemia is a documented, benign condition, and the tint builds up over weeks.

summary: Eating lots of carrots to tint the skin orange-gold; carotenemia is real but takes weeks and is a medical curiosity.
note: Orange skin can be mistaken for jaundice; it has been associated with some medical conditions.
currentQuick:
Carrot maxxing means eating lots of carrots or similar foods to give the skin a golden or orange tone. The effect it relies on, carotenemia, is real and documented.
However, the literature treats it as a harmless oddity to be told apart from jaundice, not as a cosmetic method, and no trials exist.
How it works: Carotenoids from food accumulate in the outer skin layer. Wikipedia says colour typically appears after several weeks of high intake and fades over months after stopping.
Risks and caveats: Carotenemia is generally described as benign, but it can mimic jaundice and is also associated with certain conditions such as hypothyroidism and eating disorders. A report described amenorrhea in women with diet-induced carotenemia.
deepLead:
Carrot maxxing is the looksmaxxing practice of eating large amounts of carrots or other carotenoid-rich foods to give the skin a golden or orange tint. It relies on carotenemia (also called carotenosis), a documented, benign condition in which excess dietary carotenoids accumulate in the outer skin layer .
Medical literature on carotenemia is largely clinical: case descriptions, reviews and differential diagnosis, with emphasis on distinguishing it from jaundice . No clinical studies have tested it as a cosmetic technique.

name: Tyrosine supplements for tanning

angle.text: Users take tyrosine pills or apply lotions on the theory that more of melanin's building block means a faster or deeper tan. Tyrosine's role in melanin is established biology; human trials of it for tanning have not been done.

summary: Amino-acid pills or lotion sold on the idea that more raw material means more melanin, with no human tanning trials behind it.
note: Tyrosine does not replace UV exposure for tanning; UV exposure carries skin cancer risk.
currentQuick:
L-tyrosine is a common amino acid and a building block of melanin. Some tanning products and supplement sellers suggest taking it orally or applying it topically to boost tanning.
No published human studies have tested whether it changes tanning or skin colour.
How it works: Melanocytes convert tyrosine into melanin after UV exposure. Proponents reason that extra tyrosine supplies more raw material; research has not tested whether this changes pigment in people.
Risks and caveats: Tyrosine is sold as a dietary supplement. Tanning itself involves UV exposure, which is classified as a carcinogen and causes sunburn and skin ageing.
deepLead:
Tyrosine supplements for tanning refers to the practice of taking L-tyrosine, a standard amino acid, as pills or applying it in lotions with the aim of darkening skin or speeding a tan. The idea rests on tyrosine's role as a building block of melanin, the pigment produced by melanocytes .
Tyrosine is a conditionally essential amino acid that the body makes from phenylalanine and obtains from protein-rich foods; it is also sold as a dietary supplement . Published research on supplemental tyrosine has focused on effects on neurotransmitters and performance under stress rather than on pigmentation .
No human trials of tyrosine as a tanning aid were located. The only trial record linked to the entry in the research database is unrelated to the topic (an oncology study).

name: Baby oil tanning

angle.text: Users apply baby oil before sun exposure in the belief it speeds or deepens a tan, a habit dating to the mid-twentieth century. The oils typically contain no sunscreen filter, and there are no studies behind the claimed tanning benefit.

summary: Oiling up to tan faster, a mid-century habit that adds no UV protection and has no studies behind its claimed benefit.
note: Plain oils contain no sunscreen filter; UV exposure is linked to sunburn and skin cancer.
currentQuick:
Baby oil tanning means rubbing baby oil or a tanning oil on the skin before sunbathing, with the aim of tanning faster. It was common in the 1950s and persists as a folk practice.
No studies were found testing whether plain oil improves tanning.
How it works: People do this in the belief that oil helps skin absorb or intensify sun. UV light itself drives tanning by triggering melanin production, and the oil does not change that process in any documented way.
Risks and caveats: Oils without a sunscreen filter provide no UV protection. Sunburn and UV-linked skin cancer are documented risks of sun exposure generally.
deepLead:
Baby oil tanning is the practice of applying baby oil or similar oils to the skin before sun exposure, in the belief that it speeds or deepens a tan. Because such oils typically contain no sunscreen filter, the practice is associated with greater sunburn risk .
Oils were a long-standing tanning aid: Jean Patou launched what is described as the first sun tan oil, Huile de Chaldee, in 1927, and baby oil was commonly used to increase tanning in the 1950s . Sunscreens with SPF ratings began appearing from 1962 onward, and a shift toward protective products followed .

name: Psoralen (PUVA, bergamot oil tanning)

angle.text: Psoralen and bergamot oil were used in tanning products because the compound makes skin respond more strongly to UVA, so users could darken faster. It is used medically as PUVA for skin conditions; its tanning use has been restricted, and its cosmetic tanning effect is documented mainly from that older use.

summary: A plant-derived photosensitizer that supercharges tanning under UVA; used medically as PUVA, but its tanning use was banned for phototoxic and cancer concerns.
note: Phototoxic and photocarcinogenic; tanning activators containing it were withdrawn in 1996.
currentQuick:
Psoralens are light-sensitizing compounds found in plants such as figs, celery and citrus, including bergamot oil. With UVA light they darken skin, and doctors use them in PUVA therapy for conditions like vitiligo and psoriasis.
Some tanning products once used them as accelerators; they were withdrawn in 1996.
How it works: Psoralen enters skin and, when hit by UVA, binds DNA and triggers damage responses and pigment production.
Risks and caveats: Documented harms include severe phototoxic burns and skin loss after sunbathing with psoralen products. Long-term PUVA is associated with skin cancer including melanoma, and psoralens are described as photocarcinogenic.
deepLead:
Psoralen is the parent compound of the linear furanocoumarins, plant-derived photosensitizing chemicals that bind DNA when exposed to UVA light. They occur in figs, celery, parsley, citrus fruit and, in the form of bergapten and bergamottin, in bergamot oil .
Medically, psoralen plus UVA (PUVA) is used to treat psoriasis, vitiligo and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma . In tanning culture, psoralen-containing products, including bergamot oil, have been used as tanning activators that increase pigmentation after sun exposure. Psoralen-based tanning activators were used in sun products until 1996, when they were banned after being found photocarcinogenic .
Psoralens are phototoxic: some people suffered severe skin loss after sunbathing with products containing them . Long-term PUVA treatment is associated with higher skin cancer rates, including squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma .

name: Nasal tanning spray

angle.text: Users buy nasal sprays as a needle-free way to get melanotan-style darkening without lying in the sun. The peptides involved are studied in injected form for pigment, while the nasal route for tanning has no published study.

summary: Needle-free melanotan sprays sold online; unlicensed, unregulated and untested by any published nasal-route study.
note: Unlicensed products; regulators in several countries warn against use and note possible impurities.
currentQuick:
Nasal tanning sprays are online products claiming to deliver melanotan peptides through the nose to darken skin without injections. They are not approved medicines.
No published studies were found on their effectiveness or content.
How it works: Melanotan-type peptides mimic alpha-MSH, a hormone that stimulates melanocytes to produce melanin. Whether sprays deliver meaningful amounts is undocumented in published research.
Risks and caveats: Regulators including the UK MHRA and US FDA have warned against unlicensed melanotan products. Reported effects of melanotan II include flushing, nausea and mole darkening, and product purity is unverified.
deepLead:
Nasal tanning sprays are unlicensed products, sold online, that contain melanotan-type peptides intended to darken skin when sprayed into the nose rather than injected. The active ingredients are synthetic analogues of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH), such as melanotan II .
Melanotan II was never marketed as a licensed drug, and health agencies including the UK MHRA, the Danish and Norwegian medicines agencies and the US FDA have warned against unlicensed melanotan products since 2007 . The nasal route is a variant of this broader gray market; published human research on nasal delivery for tanning was not found.

name: Sunbed + MT2 stack

angle.text: Users combine tanning-bed sessions with melanotan II to build a deep tan in fewer sessions than either alone. Each part is known to darken skin by itself, but the combination has not been trialled and rests on user reports.

summary: Pairing unlicensed melanotan with tanning beds to rush pigment; two documented-risk exposures and no trial of the combination.
note: Combines an unlicensed peptide with a Group 1 carcinogen exposure.
currentQuick:
The stack combines melanotan II, an unlicensed tanning peptide, with tanning bed sessions to darken skin faster. It circulates in looksmaxxing tanning discussions.
No studies were found testing the combination.
How it works: Melanotan II mimics alpha-MSH to stimulate melanin production, while UV light triggers tanning directly. Proponents expect the two to add together; this has not been studied.
Risks and caveats: Melanotan II is unlicensed and regulators warn against it. UV tanning devices are classified as carcinogenic and linked to higher melanoma risk; reviews note melanoma reports in melanotan users may reflect extra UV exposure.
deepLead:
The sunbed plus MT2 stack is a looksmaxxing practice of combining indoor tanning sessions with melanotan II (MT2), an unlicensed alpha-MSH analogue, with the stated goal of building pigment faster than either alone .
Melanotan II was never approved as a medicine, and health agencies have warned against unlicensed use since 2007 . UV exposure from tanning devices is classified by the WHO's IARC as a Group 1 carcinogen . Reviews of melanoma in melanotan users have said reported increases could probably be explained by heavier UV exposure . No clinical trial of the combination was found.

name: Primer tan / base tan

angle.text: People get a primer or base tan before a trip so they arrive already bronzed and, they hope, burn less. The tan itself is a visible result of UV exposure; the protection it gives has been measured as modest, around SPF 3.

summary: Tanning in advance to avoid burns later; a UV-induced tan gives only modest protection (around SPF 3) and comes from the same DNA damage.
note: The tan results from UV damage; indoor tanning is classified as carcinogenic.
currentQuick:
A primer or base tan is a tan built up before sun exposure in the belief that it will prevent later sunburn. It is often gained through gradual sun or tanning beds.
Research describes a UVB-induced tan as giving modest protection, roughly SPF 3.
How it works: UVB damages skin-cell DNA and triggers melanin production, which absorbs some UV. UVA darkening of existing melanin gives quick colour but adds no real protection.
Risks and caveats: UV exposure causes sunburn and is linked to skin cancer and ageing. Tanning devices are classified as carcinogenic to humans, and surveys found most indoor tanners had burned during sessions.
deepLead:
A primer tan or base tan is a tan acquired before a holiday or sun-heavy period, in the belief that it will protect the skin from later sunburn. It is commonly gained through gradual sun exposure or tanning bed sessions .
A UVB-induced tan does offer modest protection, roughly an SPF of about 3 according to one summary, meaning tanned skin tolerates up to about three times the exposure of pale skin . The tan itself, however, arises from UV-induced DNA damage . Surveys of young people have found that beliefs in 'safe tanning' persist .
Public health sources report that indoor tanning raises melanoma risk, and in two US surveys 58% of indoor tanners reported burns during sessions .

name: Red light tan myth

chain: Red or near-infrared light on skin
angle.text: Some looksmaxxing and skincare posters say red-light devices before sun or bed sessions prime skin to tan more readily. The idea rests on informal reasoning, and no published study of it turned up.

summary: The idea that red-light devices can 'prime' skin to tan is discussed online, but no published study on it turned up.
note: No trials found testing red light as a tanning primer.
currentQuick:
The claim holds that exposing skin to red or near-infrared light from LED panels or masks before sun or sunbed exposure prepares the skin to tan faster or deeper.
No published human studies were found that test this specific idea. Red light devices are generally studied for other purposes, such as wound healing and pain.
How it works: Proponents of the idea generally suggest that red light stimulates skin cells in a way that boosts pigment response. Encyclopedic sources on red light therapy do not describe tanning or melanin effects; they describe photobiomodulation as an area still under investigation.[1]
Risks and caveats: Red light devices are cleared by the FDA for some uses, and some users report mild irritation or pain; long-term skin effects are described as not known.[1] Tanning with UV carries its own documented risks, including sunburn and increased skin cancer risk.[2]
deepLead:
The red light tan claim is the belief, circulated in looksmaxxing and skincare circles, that treating skin with red or near-infrared light before UV exposure primes it to tan more readily. It is a fringe idea in the sense that its proponents rely mostly on informal reasoning rather than published research.
Red light therapy, also called low-level laser therapy or photobiomodulation, uses low-power lasers or LEDs and has been studied mainly for wound healing and pain; a 2012 review cited by Wikipedia found inconsistent, low-quality evidence for chronic wounds. The Wikipedia article on the topic does not discuss tanning or pigmentation.
No published clinical study was located that tests red light as a tan primer. Natural tanning is described by encyclopedic sources as driven by UV radiation acting on melanocytes.

name: Tan lines meta

angle.text: Users manage tan lines on purpose, either evening them out for a seamless bronze look or showing them off as a style detail. The result is immediately visible; it is a presentation choice with no clinical research behind it.

summary: Deliberately showing, hiding or evening out tan lines for a better-looking tan, a style detail with no clinical research behind it.
note: Methods that add UV exposure carry sunburn and skin cancer risk.
currentQuick:
Tan lines are the contrast between skin exposed to sun and skin covered by clothing or swimwear. Some people try to avoid them with tan-through clothing or sun exposure of covered areas, while others keep them for effect.
No clinical studies on tan line management as an appearance strategy were found.
How it works: Tanning occurs when melanocytes make melanin in response to UV; covered skin does not receive UV, so it stays lighter.[1] People managing tan lines adjust clothing, positioning or use sunless tanners to even out colour.[2]
Risks and caveats: Added UV exposure to even a tan raises the risk of sunburn, premature aging and skin cancer.[1] Sunless products avoid UV but can streak or look orange if applied unevenly, and bronzers can rub off on clothing.[2]
deepLead:
Tan lines are visible boundaries between tanned skin and skin that was covered, for example by swimwear or a watch strap. In appearance-focused communities, the term 'tan lines meta' refers to deliberately managing them, either to avoid them for an even tan or to display them.
Tan-through swimwear was introduced in 1969, and a Coppertone advertisement from 1953 famously depicted a child's tan line, according to Wikipedia. Sunless tanning products are another route to evening out colour without added UV exposure.

name: Vitamin D / UVB for tan

chain: Vitamin D forms and pigment rises
angle.text: Some people frame UVB sun exposure as serving two goals at once: vitamin D production and a tan. UVB is known to drive both, and the entry separates the two aims since each is pursued for different reasons.

summary: The overlap between sun-for-vitamin-D and sun-for-a-tan: UVB does both, but they are separate goals.
note: UV exposure raises sunburn and skin cancer risk; vitamin D can also come from diet or supplements.
currentQuick:
UVB radiation in sunlight both stimulates new melanin (tanning) and drives vitamin D production in skin. Some people cite vitamin D as a reason for sun or sunbed exposure that also gives them a tan.
Small registered trials have measured vitamin D after sunbed or UVB exposure, but this article does not rely on their results.
How it works: UVB converts a skin precursor into vitamin D3.[1] Melanin absorbs UV and inhibits UVB-driven vitamin D synthesis, which is why darker skin makes less for the same exposure.[1] UVB also stimulates new melanin, producing a tan that appears two to three days later.[2]
Risks and caveats: Excess UV is linked to sunburn, skin aging, DNA damage and skin cancer.[2] Wikipedia notes vitamin D can also come from diet and supplements, and health bodies publish intake guidance.[1]
deepLead:
Vitamin D / UVB for tan refers to the overlap between exposing skin to ultraviolet B radiation for vitamin D production and doing so to obtain a tan. UVB converts a precursor in the skin into vitamin D3, which for most people supplies more vitamin D than diet.
The same UVB band prompts melanocytes to make new melanin, which appears a few days after exposure. Melanin in turn absorbs UV and reduces UVB-driven vitamin D synthesis.
Several small trials of UVB, sunbeds and supplementation have been registered; this article describes their topics only. Public health bodies set intake recommendations for vitamin D that do not depend on tanning.

name: Tanning oil

angle.text: Users apply tanning oil while sunbathing to deepen colour and give skin a glossy bronzed finish. The tan comes from sun exposure, and oils have been used for this since the 1920s; sunless DHA oils give colour without UV.

summary: Oils applied before sun exposure to deepen a tan, often with little or no SPF; sunless DHA oils also exist.
note: Oils with low or no SPF offer little protection against sunburn.
currentQuick:
Tanning oils are cosmetic oils applied to skin in the sun. Historically they were marketed to speed or deepen tanning, with Jean Patou's 1927 product described as the first, and baby oil was common in the 1950s.
A newer category blends oils with DHA for sunless colour. No clinical trials of tanning oils for appearance were found.
How it works: Sun-exposure oils do not themselves darken skin; tanning comes from UV acting on melanocytes.[1] DHA-based oils colour the dead outer skin layer through a browning reaction without UV.[2]
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia notes sunburn is the most common UV hazard and excess exposure raises skin cancer risk.[1] Products without sunscreen offer less protection, and DHA colour does not protect from UV.[2]
deepLead:
Tanning oil is a cosmetic oil applied to the skin while sunbathing, traditionally intended to encourage tanning. Wikipedia credits Jean Patou's 1927 'Huile de Chaldee' as the first sun tan oil and notes baby oil was widely used in the 1950s to increase tanning.
Product patents also describe sunless oil-in-water emulsions combining DHA with vegetable oils. Sunless tanners based on DHA tint the skin's outer layer without UV.
No clinical trials of tanning oils as appearance products were located. Sunscreen availability has been examined in a cross-sectional US study, which is not specific to tanning oils.

name: Tanning drops (Isle of Paradise style)

angle.text: Users mix self-tan drops into their moisturiser to choose how deep and how gradual a tan looks, building colour over days. The colour change is visible within hours; there is no independent research on the drops as a format.

summary: Self-tan concentrate drops mixed into a moisturiser to build a custom colour, with no independent research on them.
note: DHA colour is temporary and fades in about 3 to 10 days.
currentQuick:
Tanning drops are concentrated self-tanning products added to a person's own lotion or skincare so that colour deepens with the amount used. Isle of Paradise is one brand associated with the format.
The format is not discussed in the encyclopedic sources reviewed, and no clinical studies were found.
How it works: Self-tanners generally rely on DHA, which reacts with amino acids in the dead outer layer of skin in a Maillard-type browning reaction, with no UV or melanin involved.[1]
Risks and caveats: DHA colour fades over roughly 3 to 10 days, and misapplication can produce orange or splotchy results.[1] Skin may be more UV-susceptible for about 24 hours after DHA use, and contact dermatitis is reported.[1]
deepLead:
Tanning drops are concentrated sunless tanning products designed to be mixed into moisturiser, serum or other skincare, letting the user adjust colour intensity. The format is associated with brands such as Isle of Paradise.
Sunless tanners usually contain dihydroxyacetone (DHA) at about 3 to 5 percent, which reacts with amino acids in the dead outer skin layer; the colour is temporary and does not involve melanin or UV. Wikipedia's article on sunless tanning does not mention drops specifically.
No clinical studies on tanning drops were found.

name: Tanning wipes / towelettes

angle.text: Users reach for tanning wipes for a quick, portable way to add bronzed colour without a mitt or bottle. The colour shows up as it develops and is temporary; no clinical trials of the wipes are published.

summary: Pre-soaked DHA wipes for quick self-tan application; temporary colour with no published clinical trials.
note: Colour is temporary and can streak; DHA is not approved for use around eyes or lips.
currentQuick:
Tanning wipes are pre-moistened cloths impregnated with a self-tanning composition, such as DHA, that are wiped over the skin for convenience.
A patent filing describes the concept, but no clinical studies of the product category were found.
How it works: Wipes deliver the same kind of DHA colour as other self-tanners, which reacts with the dead outer skin layer and fades in about 3 to 10 days.[1]
Risks and caveats: Uneven wiping can cause streaking or orange colour, and DHA is not approved around eyes, lips or mucous membranes.[1] Bronzers may rub off on clothing.[1]
deepLead:
Tanning wipes, or towelettes, are tissues pre-soaked with a self-tanning or bronzing composition for application by wiping. A patent filing describes a tanning aid made of tissue paper impregnated with a tanning lotion, tanning oil or bronzing agent.
Self-tanning products commonly use DHA, which colours the dead outer layer of skin without UV and fades within roughly 3 to 10 days.
No clinical studies on tanning wipes were found.
